forecasts.question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2030?
forecasts.key_change: Down 1pp to 22%. Quiet 3-day window since 17 May with no fresh AGI declaration. Air Street's May State of AI and llm-stats updates confirm continued capability gains (GPT-5.5-Cyber for vetted defenders; Anthropic's $1.5B JV with Blackstone/Goldman/General Atlantic) but nothing crossing the 3+ leading-researcher threshold. Amodei (Davos 2026) continues to point to 2027 as his modal AGI year, leaving roughly 31 months to deadline. Resolution mechanics — a public lab announcement OR 3+ leading researcher attestations — remain demanding; the OpenAI/Microsoft renegotiation has explicitly displaced 'AGI' with granular capability gates, weakening lab-side incentives to declare. Modest 1pp drift down reflects the time decay without offsetting signal.
forecasts.base_rate: Reference class — major paradigm-defining technology claims with 31-month horizons resolved YES historically <20%. Researcher surveys (2023-2025) median AGI year clusters 2040-2047.

factors_up.factor: Continued frontier capability gains (Mythos Preview, GPT-5.5 cyber, agentic coding scaling)
Amodei publicly anchoring 2027 AGI in Davos — increases probability of lab-led declaration race
Anthropic-Blackstone-Goldman JV deploying Claude at enterprise scale may compress capability discovery loops

factors_down.factor: OpenAI removing 'AGI' clause from Microsoft contract — explicit deprecation of the term as resolution-relevant
No researcher consensus near a YES-triggering threshold
31 months is short relative to typical capability-to-claim lag in foundational technology

key_uncertainties: Whether lab marketing pressure will produce a self-declared 'AGI' claim before genuine consensus
How resolution will treat partial capability demonstrations (e.g. economically-valuable autonomous task completion at human level)
Speed of agentic R&D loop self-acceleration
update_triggers: Any leading lab publicly declaring AGI achieved
Coordinated statement from 2+ leading researchers near the 3-researcher threshold
Major capability benchmark (e.g. ARC-AGI v3) cleared at human-expert level

forecasts.question: Will economic consultancy lose ≥33% value/jobs by end 2030 due to AI?
forecasts.key_change: Down 1pp to 24%. Fast Company and Inc. follow-ups this week reframe McKinsey's late-2025 200-role cut and Sternfels' signalled ~10% non-client reduction as the *leading edge* of a structural shift, not a one-off. McKinsey total headcount now down to ~40,000 with revenue gains stalling. KPMG, Deloitte, Bain, Accenture all running parallel AI-assistant rollouts and selective workforce redesigns. But: cumulative observed cuts remain well under the 33% threshold (closer to 5-10% across the named firms), and 'primarily attributed to AI by 2+ credible analyses' is a high evidentiary bar. The trajectory is consistent with a 33% impact by 2030, but year-on-year deceleration in the cuts and offsetting AI-services revenue keep the central estimate in the low-twenties.
forecasts.base_rate: Reference class — professional services industries losing 33%+ to a single technology within 5 years historically <15% (closest analogue: travel agents, paralegals, both >5-year transitions).

factors_up.factor: McKinsey 10% cut over 2 years signalled + revenue stagnation — extrapolates to >33% if compounded with weak top-line
Big Four AI assistants now production-deployed for staff, reducing leverage ratios
Junior analyst pyramid economics most exposed — output that took weeks now minutes

factors_down.factor: Headcount cuts to date <10%, far below 33% threshold
Firms substituting consulting revenue with AI-implementation/transformation services — top line resilience
Resolution requires 2+ credible analyses primarily attributing decline to AI — substantial evidentiary friction

key_uncertainties: Whether economic-consultancy-specific data will be disaggregated from broader management consulting
How much AI-services revenue offsets traditional consulting decline
Whether 'value' is measured by revenue, headcount, billings, or some composite
update_triggers: MCA, Source Global, or Kennedy publishing 2026 sector-wide revenue/headcount data
Another tier-1 firm announcing >15% cuts in a single round
Major analyst report quantifying AI's primary causal contribution to a decline

forecasts.question: Will Labour be largest party at next UK General Election?
forecasts.key_change: Down 1pp to 2%. YouGov 10-11 May poll is a clear deterioration: Reform 28%, Conservatives 17%, Greens 16%, Labour 16%, Lib Dems 13% — Labour now in *fourth place* nationally, with a 12pp gap to Reform. PollCheck 7-poll moving average (19 May) confirms the shift: Reform 27.7%, Conservatives 18.3%, Labour 17.6%. Labour has now fallen behind the Conservatives in the moving average, a meaningful regime change. With seats projections from Electoral Calculus and others now showing Reform winning a plurality or majority on these vote shares, and the next GE not legally required until Aug 2029 (typical scheduling Dec 2029), Labour would need to recover 10+ points to become largest party — possible but increasingly unlikely on the current trajectory.
forecasts.base_rate: Reference class — UK incumbent governments trailing by >10pp 3+ years from election, becoming largest party at the following GE: roughly 25-30% historically.

factors_up.factor: 3+ years until probable election leaves ample recovery time
Reform's vote share historically volatile — UKIP analog peaked 18 months before 2015 GE and collapsed
Labour incumbency benefits — patronage, dispatch box, policy delivery window

factors_down.factor: Labour now in 4th place in latest YouGov, 12pp behind Reform
Labour fallen below Conservatives in moving average — symbolic threshold breached
Reform's consolidation of right-of-centre + economically-discontented voters appears structural, not protest

key_uncertainties: Whether Reform's lead is durable or peaks 12-18 months pre-election (UKIP precedent)
Possibility of Reform-Conservative pact splitting (or consolidating) the right
Labour leadership question — replacement of Starmer would reset polling
update_triggers: Labour polling consistently above 22% in 3+ pollsters (turnaround signal)
Reform-Conservative formal pact announcement
Major Reform scandal or leadership change
Labour leadership challenge

forecasts.question: Will China initiate a military blockade or invasion of Taiwan before 1 January 2030?
forecasts.key_change: Hold at 7%. AEI 15 May update notes continuing PLA Southern Theater pressure but the Xi-Trump summit (13-15 May) — while reaching no major Taiwan agreements — established a direct leader-level channel that historically de-escalates near-term kinetic risk. No new escalation triggers in the 3-day window since 17 May. The Diplomat's January 2026 piece flagging the 12-nautical-mile normalisation strategy remains the dominant medium-term concern but is consistent with grey-zone coercion, not the >72hr blockade/assault threshold required for YES. Justice Mission 2025 rehearsed full blockade capability in late December 2025, signalling continued readiness. Holding at 7%: structural risk elevated, but short-term diplomatic temperature lower.
forecasts.base_rate: Major-power initiated kinetic action against a defended democracy in any given ~4 year window historically <5%. Taiwan-specific premium given 21st century PLA modernisation: +3-5pp.

factors_up.factor: Justice Mission 2025 demonstrated full blockade rehearsal capability
Steady normalisation of PLA activity in Taiwan's 12nm contiguous zone lowering escalation thresholds
PRC undersea seabed mapping suggests amphibious/submarine operational planning
Xi political incentive to act before potential 2027-2028 succession transition

factors_down.factor: Xi-Trump May 2026 leader-level direct channel reduces near-term miscalculation risk
Taiwan defensive posture (asymmetric weapons, US backing under MDIA 2023) raises cost of YES action
PRC economic vulnerability to global sanctions in invasion scenario
Historical base rate of major-power kinetic action low even when capability present

key_uncertainties: Xi's read of US deterrence credibility under Trump second term
Whether grey-zone coercion succeeds without kinetic escalation
Internal PRC economic/political pressures affecting risk tolerance
update_triggers: Withdrawal of US military from First Island Chain
PLA forward deployment exceeding exercise patterns (e.g. mass mobilisation, civilian shipping requisitioning)
Major Taiwan political crisis (e.g. independence referendum)
Breakdown of US-PRC leader-level diplomacy

forecasts.question: Will UK annual CPI inflation fall below 2.0% for at least one month before 1 January 2027?
forecasts.key_change: Up 2pp to 3%. Material new data: ONS April 2026 CPI release (published this morning) showed annual CPI rate at 2.8%, DOWN from 3.3% in March 2026 — a substantial 0.5pp single-month fall, the largest in over a year. Driven by housing/household services (energy price reversal as Middle East spike eased) plus base effects. CPIH at 3.0% (down from 3.4%). With only 8 monthly prints remaining before 1 Jan 2027 (May, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep, Oct, Nov, Dec 2026), reaching <2.0% in any single month requires sustained downward momentum of ~0.1pp/month, which is achievable but not central. Core inflation still above 3% suggests stickiness. Probability remains low but the April surprise meaningfully lifts the tail. Maintain CI ceiling of 9%.
forecasts.base_rate: Reference class — UK CPI annual rate falling 0.8pp+ in 8 months from a starting level of 2.8%: roughly 15-25% in historic post-2000 data, higher in disinflation episodes.

factors_up.factor: April 2026 print 2.8% — only 0.8pp from threshold, lowest in over a year
Energy base effects in H2 2026 favourable (high 2025 comparator)
BoE rate trajectory still restrictive — cumulative monetary policy lag biting

factors_down.factor: Core inflation still >3%, indicating services/wage-driven stickiness
Only 8 monthly prints remaining — short window for sustained disinflation
Geopolitical (Middle East, Russia) and supply-chain risks to energy prices
Fiscal loosening risk into late 2026 if Reform pressure forces giveaways

key_uncertainties: Whether April's drop is base-effect noise or trend
Pace of services inflation deceleration
Energy price stability through autumn 2026
update_triggers: May 2026 CPI print on track in mid-June
Energy price shock (oil spike, gas disruption)
BoE policy pivot signalling sub-2% target proximity

forecasts.question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
forecasts.key_change: Hold at 37%. Raedan Institute's May 2026 outlook and Commons Library briefing both reiterate OBR's March 2026 EFO assumptions: GDP growth 1.1% (2026), 1.6% (2027); GDP per person 1.1% pa average 2026-2030. IFS economic outlook flags 'narrow paths' for productivity. With OBR's TFP assumption held at 0.8% but labour supply growth falling to 0.5% by 2030 (lower migration, ageing), total potential growth converges around 1.3-1.4% — below the 1.5% threshold. For the 2030s average to clear 1.5%, the UK would need either a sustained productivity surprise (TFP back to 1.0%+) or a labour supply reversal. Both possible — particularly if AI-driven productivity gains materialise — but base rate suggests they're roughly 50-50 propositions individually, ~35-40% combined. Hold at 37%.
forecasts.base_rate: Reference class — UK rolling 10-year real GDP growth >1.5% since 2010: realised roughly 40% of starting decades.

factors_up.factor: AI-driven productivity gains could lift TFP back above 1.0%
Possible policy reset post-2029 GE (Reform fiscal expansion, planning reform)
OBR explicitly notes potential output understated if investment surprises

factors_down.factor: OBR labour supply growth declining to 0.5% by 2030 — structural drag
TFP assumption 0.8% — well below pre-GFC ~2% trajectory
Climate-transition costs and ageing-population fiscal pressure

key_uncertainties: Whether AI-driven productivity actually shows up in measured GDP (Solow paradox concerns)
Net migration trajectory under future governments
Post-2030 climate-transition capex impact on GDP measurement
update_triggers: OBR major TFP assumption revision
Net migration policy change
Productivity statistics surprise (ONS quarterly releases)
Major AI-productivity empirical study (BoE, OECD, IMF)
